question: Big-O Notation
content: Big-O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm\'s time complexity as input size grows, focusing on worst-case scenario.
description: You are evaluating if an administrative filing system will scale as your company grows from 10 to 10,000 employees. What should you consider?
options: How the time required to find files grows with the number of files - look for logarithmic or linear growth rather than quadratic or worse
Only the current speed of the system
The aesthetic design of the filing cabinets
The color of the file folders
answer: How the time required to find files grows with the number of files - look for logarithmic or linear growth rather than quadratic or worse
explanation: Big-O notation helps you understand how an algorithm\'s performance scales. For searching, you want O(log n) (binary search) or O(n) (linear search), not O(n^2) or worse which would become unusably slow at scale.

question: Bubble Sort
content: Bubble Sort repeatedly steps through a list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
description: You have a messy pile of laundry to sort by color. How would you apply Bubble Sort?
options: Compare each pair of adjacent items and swap them if they\'re in the wrong color order, repeating passes through the pile until no swaps are needed
Throw all clothes in the pile and hope they sort themselves
Sort by throwing each item onto one of several pre-decided piles
Wear all clothes at once to avoid sorting
answer: Compare each pair of adjacent items and swap them if they\'re in the wrong color order, repeating passes through the pile until no swaps are needed
explanation: Bubble Sort works by repeatedly swapping adjacent elements that are out of order. For laundry, you\'d compare each pair of adjacent items and swap them if, for example, a darker item is before a lighter one when sorting light to dark.

question: Insertion Sort
content: Insertion Sort builds a sorted array one item at a time by taking each new item and inserting it into the correct position in the already-sorted part.
description: You are organizing a book collection on a shelf as you acquire new books one by one. How would Insertion Sort work?
options: Place each new book in its correct alphabetical position among the books already on the shelf
Stack all new books in a pile and sort them all at once monthly
Arrange books by the height of the spine rather than title
Leave books wherever they fall when you put them down
answer: Place each new book in its correct alphabetical position among the books already on the shelf
explanation: Insertion Sort is like organizing books as you get them: for each new book, you compare it to the books already on the shelf from right to left until you find where it belongs, then insert it there.

question: Merge Sort
content: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that splits data into halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges the sorted halves.
description: You are managing a large team project with multiple independent components. How could Merge Sort principles apply?
options: Divide the project into independent pods, have each pod complete their work, then integrate (merge) the completed components
Have everyone work on every task simultaneously
Randomly assign tasks without regard to dependencies
Do all tasks in alphabetical order by task name
answer: Divide the project into independent pods, have each pod complete their work, then integrate (merge) the completed components
explanation: Merge Sort\'s divide-and-conquer approach maps to project management: split work into independent chunks (divide), let each team complete their chunk (conquer/sort), then combine the finished work (merge).

question: Search Costs
content: Search costs refer to the time and effort required to find an item in a collection, which depends on how the collection is organized.
description: You\'re deciding whether to spend time organizing your desk or leave papers in a pile. What factor should influence your decision?
options: How frequently you need to find specific items - if retrieval is rare, organizing may not be worth the effort
Only whether the pile looks messy to visitors
The color of your desk
The phase of the moon
answer: How frequently you need to find specific items - if retrieval is rare, organizing may not be worth the effort
explanation: The sort/search tradeoff: organizing (sorting) has upfront cost but reduces future search cost. If you rarely need to find specific items, the effort of organizing may exceed the time saved from faster searches.

question: Linear Search
content: Linear Search checks each element in a list sequentially until the target is found or the end is reached.
description: You\'re looking for a specific screwdriver in a completely chaotic, unorganized garage toolbox. What search method are you using?
options: Checking each tool one by one until you find the right screwdriver
Using a magnetic tool finder
Asking the screwdriver to call out when you\'re near
Waiting for the screwdriver to float to the top of the pile
answer: Checking each tool one by one until you find the right screwdriver
explanation: In an unsorted collection with no indexing, Linear Search (checking each item sequentially) is your only option. You examine each tool until you find the target screwdriver.

question: Binary Search
content: Binary Search efficiently finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half.
description: You\'re looking for a name in a massive, alphabetized physical registration logbook. How should you search?
options: Open the book to the middle, check if the name comes before or after that point, then repeat the process in the relevant half
Start at page one and read every name until you find it
Guess a page number and hope the name is there
Lick your finger and hold it up to see which way the wind blows
answer: Open the book to the middle, check if the name comes before or after that point, then repeat the process in the relevant half
explanation: Binary Search works on sorted data: check the middle item, eliminate half the remaining possibilities based on comparison, and repeat. For an alphabetized list, you compare alphabetically to decide which half to search next.

question: Inversion Count
content: Inversion Count measures how far a list is from being sorted by counting pairs of elements that are out of order.
description: You\'ve created a music playlist that\'s supposed to follow a specific thematic flow, but the order seems off. How could you quantify how \'messed up\' it is?
options: Count how many pairs of songs are in the wrong order relative to the intended sequence
Count only the songs that are in the correct position
Measure the total playback time of the playlist
See how many songs start with the letter \'A\'
answer: Count how many pairs of songs are in the wrong order relative to the intended sequence
explanation: An inversion is a pair of elements that are out of their natural order. The total inversion count quantifies how disordered a sequence is - a sorted list has zero inversions, a reverse-sorted list has maximum inversions.

question: Social Hierarchies
content: In animal societies, dominance hierarchies (pecking orders) reduce conflict by establishing known relationships, minimizing costly fights.
description: How might ancient tracking of pecking orders in chicken societies have reduced physical violence?
options: By allowing chickens to assess dominance visually without fighting, once the hierarchy was established
By making all chickens equally aggressive
By eliminating the concept of chicken social order
By forcing chickens to wear blindfolds
answer: By allowing chickens to assess dominance visually without fighting, once the hierarchy was established
explanation: Once a pecking order is established through initial confrontations, chickens can recognize their relative positions and avoid fights by yielding to higher-ranked individuals, reducing the need for ongoing violence.

question: Pre-Sorting Value
content: Pre-sorting value considers whether sorting items earlier (e.g., on receipt) provides enough benefit to justify the effort compared to sorting later (e.g., before shipping).
description: You\'re managing a warehouse and deciding whether to sort incoming inventory immediately or wait until orders are ready to ship. What should you consider?
options: Whether sorting now reduces overall effort compared to sorting later, considering factors like order frequency and item similarity
Only the color of the incoming boxes
The phase of the moon when items arrive
Always sort immediately regardless of circumstances
answer: Whether sorting now reduces overall effort compared to sorting later, considering factors like order frequency and item similarity
explanation: The decision depends on comparing total effort: if you sort items once when they\'ll be needed in sorted order multiple times, pre-sorting wins. If items ship in unsorted orders frequently, post-sorting or no sorting may be better.
